en: The Ritual Manual for the Yoga Practice of the Uṣṇīṣavijayā Buddha-Crown, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha. 1.
Chapter on the Preface: The Preface to the Uṣṇīṣavijayā Dhāraṇī. Chapter One.
I prostrate to all the Bhagavāns, and to Akṣobhya,
the heroic and fierce Vajra of the Eastern Vajra Family, as well as Vajragarbha;
to Ratnasambhava Tathāgata, Ākāśagarbha, Ratnākara, Amitāyus, and Avalokiteśvararāja, the Lotus-Eyed One.
Viśvakarman, the Great Muni; Amoghasiddhi, the Honored Sattva;
The four Pāramitās and the four Offerings; The eight Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Wheel-Turning Kings— For the benefit of all practitioners of yoga, may they swiftly attain the supreme great siddhi.
Delighting in the practice of the signless, he teaches yoga; Seeking that which possesses signs, he further explains that signs and their absence are of one essence in true, great emptiness.
Therefore, I now practice yoga through the contemplation of syllables to realize the wisdom of the true mark;
The three kinds of prajñā are not of a single essence.
The three mysteries of body, speech, and mind are the gates; the manifested and the dharma-body are themselves the three mysteries.
The five wheels are the wheels of the five wisdoms; through the five wisdoms, the five bodies are realized.
The five wheels completely encompass the wheel of the dharma-realm; for the three mysteries are the three bodies.
Therefore, I now pay homage to Yoga; Yoga is indeed the Venerable Mahāvairocana.
Therefore, I now practice Yoga for the benefit of all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm, and shall now briefly explain the method of the Honored and Supreme Dhāraṇī.
This means that it removes all obstacles and extinguishes all rebirths in the hells and as animals;
therefore, it is called the meaning of the Uṣṇīṣavijayā Buddha-Crown.
For this reason, the Tathāgata [spoke] for the sake of the Devaputra Susamsthita.
It is said that after seven lifetimes as an animal have been eliminated,
this practitioner of yoga differs from those of ordinary methods;
if they realize the unborn in a single moment, [they attain liberation].
The five wisdoms are transformed into the fivefold Dharma-body;
awakening to the three mysteries is itself the three bodies.
At the very moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, one transcends the one hundred and sixty types of mental states.
Having completed the practice throughout three incalculable eons,
he realized the Samādhi of the Universal Manifestation of the Physical Body;
this is precisely what is meant by attaining perfect enlightenment at the very moment of first generating the bodhicitta.
Therefore, for those who seek that which possesses signs,
I now teach that which possesses signs;
for those who seek the signless, I further teach the method of recitation for the signless.
Although many types have been taught,
I shall now briefly explain two that encompass all of them:
the first is for the purpose of seeking worldly benefits such as the removal of calamities and the increase of prosperity.
Briefly stated, there are two aspects to the dharmas with signs:
for those practitioners of yoga who seek unexcelled bodhi,
one teaches the dharma of the sudden entry into the universal manifestation of the form-body (rūpakāya) through non-arising.
There are briefly four types of worldly recitation:
namely, those for averting calamities, increasing prosperity, subjugating, and summoning;
these correspond respectively to square, circular, triangular, and crescent-shaped maṇḍalas.
The method for the homa hearth is as follows:
there are four types of recitation.
When performing the recitation for enrichment (puṣṭi):
At the beginning and end of every mantra,
add the two characters *na* and *mo*.
This applies when reciting for the purpose of averting calamities.
Add the two syllables *svāhā* at the beginning and end of the mantra.
When performing the recitation for subjugation (*abhicāra*),
add the three syllables *hūṃ phaṭ*.
When performing the recitation for summoning,
one should add the two syllables *hā* and *ri* (𑖧𑖿𑖪𑖿) before and after each mantra;
this constitutes the phrases for averting calamities, increasing prosperity, subjugating, and summoning.
One should also recite the names of those being visualized.
As for their physical characteristics, they are yellow, white, red, and blue;
alternatively, one may visualize the faces, the entire bodies, and the clothing as being their respective natural colors.
All offerings— incense, flowers, powdered incense, and ointments—
as well as various foods and drinks, whether yellow, white, red, or blue, fragrant, sweet, bland, or pungent—
should each be prepared in accordance with the corresponding original ritual methods.

Regarding the various distinct methods for *homa* and other rites, as well as the specific types of wood to be used for burning, one must also consult the relevant root text at the time of practice and perform them accordingly.
Chapter Two: The Rules for Recitation (*Japa*). Furthermore, when one wishes to perform the ritual of recitation, [one should proceed as follows].
First, one must enter the samādhi of the pure dharma-realm.
Visualize the syllable *lāṃ* upon the crown of the head;
it is triangular in shape and consists of the fire of wisdom.
The body is like the sun first rising;
the entire body is consumed by the fire of wisdom, burning away the four great elements and the five aggregates, leaving only emptiness and stillness.
The mantra of that dharmadhātu is as follows:
*Namo samantabuddhānām raṃ*. Recite this with mind and mouth while visualizing the crown of the head and the entire body as a triangular shape of wisdom-fire, as shown in the diagram above.
Next, one enters the *pañcacakrasamādhi* (the meditative absorption of the five wheels).
He then entered the *vajramaṇḍala-samādhi*.
He visualized the area below his own navel as being square, purple-gold in color,
and serving as a *vajramaṇḍala*.
Then, one recites the mantra:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām*. When visualizing each syllable, such as *A*, one simultaneously recites it aloud while taking refuge.
Visualize the seed-syllable as the essential body;
its form is as shown in the diagram.
The syllable A is a yellow vajra-wheel.
Next, visualize the syllable 𑖮 (va) at the navel.
It is the water-wheel of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), the color of a conch shell or like the color of milk,
and its shape is like the full moon.
As shown in the illustration below:
the mantra for the water wheel (*vāruṇa-cakra*) is *Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ vaṃ*.
Next, the mantra for the fire wheel (*tejocakra*) is explained as follows:
*Namo samantabuddhānām*. On the heart center, visualize a triangular wheel of fire.
Its color is like that of the newly risen sun, and its blazing flames are as fierce and sharp as the fire at the end of an aeon (*kalpāgni*).
Its shape is like a triangular maṇḍala.
Next, visualize the syllable *ha*,
which has the form of a bindu in the great void (*mahāśūnya*) and is black in color, shaped like a crescent moon facing upward.
The name is "Containing" (Saṃgraha).
This is the celestial wind-circle,
positioned above the eyebrows, dark and heavy like the winds at the end of an eon.
Next, one contemplates the syllable *khaṃ* at the crown of the head.
It is the Great Space Wheel (*mahākha-cakra*), endowed with all colors and various forms;
it is called the Great Space Wheel.
This is called the wheel of the five wisdoms,
namely earth, water, fire, wind, and space.
One should then empower the five limbs with the universal mudrā.
One immediately attains true wisdom.
Then, the common mantra is recited:
Oṃ sarvathāḥ utpannate sapraheṣe gagana-kaṃ svāhā. Next, with the hands of concentration and wisdom, one interlaces the ten fingers.
By placing [the hand] upon the crown and applying it to the five limbs,
one immediately attains the indestructible vajra body,
for one has entered the samaya.
One becomes identical with the samaya-body of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
manifesting as the samaya-body, one performs the Buddha-deeds.
First, one enters the samādhi of the samaya.
The mantra is:
Oṃ vajra-jvala samaya-mekha. Recite this mantra while performing the empowerment upon each seal-imprint.
As for the characteristic of this mudrā, the wisdom and dhyāna hands are interlaced;
with palms joined level at the navel, the wisdom hand presses down upon the dhyāna hand.
This is called the Samaya-mudrā of the Heart of All Buddhas.
Because all mudrās arise from forming this mudrā,
one first forms it and emerges from the samaya;
this is equivalent to being empowered at the five places by the samaya.
The crown of the head and the throat are designated as the five limbs.
The diagrams of these five wheels are as shown to the left.
The great space-bindu possesses various colors.
The syllable *khaṃ* is named the wind element, the syllable *laṃ* the fire element, the syllable *vaṃ* the water element, and the syllable *aḥ* the earth element.
The vajra-wheel is at the waist,
and the great space-wheel is at the crown of the head.
The wind-wheel is above the eyebrows;
the fire-wheel is at the heart;
the water-wheel is at the navel.

In one version of this text, this illustration is absent. Once the five aggregates (*skandha*) and four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of conditioned existence have been transcended, one establishes the unconditioned, indestructible diamond-like five aggregates;
these are then termed the body of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna-kāya*), which is itself unconditioned.
The ground of the maṇḍala is likewise.
That maṇḍala is empowered by the five wheels,
which are named earth, water, fire, wind, and space.
Based on the five great elements of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), one establishes the five great elements of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Therefore, when first observing the characteristics of the maṇḍala ground,
one first rises from space and contemplates wind and the other elements as shown in the diagram to the left.
With the mind of the pure *dharmadhātu*,
first burn away all impurities, defilements, and contaminations within the site of the maṇḍala;
thereafter, establish the five great wheels (*pañcamahācakra*) in their proper sequence.
Immediately, one should perform the boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*) to protect the body and expel obstructors;
then, manifesting and purifying the three karmas, one should firmly establish the bodhicitta and so forth.
For this reason, one again enters the mantra and mudrā of the Vajrasamaya.
The mantra is: Oṃ vajra bandha traṭ. As for the mudrā:
perform the aforementioned Vajrapāṇi mudrā.
Then, form a fist and place it upon the heart.
While fixing the mind there, open the clenched fist and lower both hands three times while binding them.
This is called the Vajradhātu-mudrā.
Having thus bound the mind in three ways,
by the power of these mantras and mudrās,
one is able to purify the three karmas and stabilize the bodhicitta.
Next, at the place of recitation, one should dispel impurities and obstructing spirits.
Whatever incense, flowers, unguents, powdered incense, and various offerings are presented shall be used to expel defilements,
radiate light, and increase majestic power.
Form the Vajradhātu mudrā to demarcate the boundaries of all directions,
to protect oneself and one's companions, and to guard one's dwelling place,
as previously described, including those points not yet detailed.
When facing any task, one must recite this mantra and perform the mudrā for protection in every instance;
this will ensure accomplishment free from all obstacles and difficulties.
One should empower [the rite] with the mantra and hand-seal of the Trailokyavijaya (Conqueror of the Three Worlds).
Each is capable of accomplishing all activities and so forth.
Next, recite the mantra of Trailokyavijaya:
Oṃ niḥ svā vajra hūṃ. This is called the speech and hand-seal (mudrā) of the Honored One Trailokyavijaya.
He is named Sarvakarmasādhaka.
His mudrā consists of the wisdom-samādhi fists,
with the vāyu-finger raised like a banner.
Bend the two great space-wheels (thumb and ring finger) into the palms and press them with the earth, water, and fire wheels (middle, index, and little fingers); thus the seal is formed.
As for this mudrā, place the hand of concentration upon the heart.
Using the seal of wisdom (*jñānamudrā*),
touch all objects and bind the boundaries of the four directions as well as the upper and lower realms.
By circling three times clockwise, the boundaries from top to bottom are established.
Chapter Three: Invoking the Principal Deity and Others. Furthermore, one should then invoke all the Buddhas, the eight great Cakravartin Uṣṇīṣa kings, or the principal deities of one’s own family.
Arising from the samaya, he gazes about;
out of compassion for the mantra-practitioner,
he descends to the ritual arena.
The mantra for generating [the deity] is:
Oṃ vajra tiṣṭha. As for the form of its mudrā: the hands of wisdom and concentration [are joined].
The earth-wheels are linked together like a chain;
one causes the great space to enter the palms.
Then, with the water-wheel and the fire-wheel, one presses down upon both sides of the space-wheel.
The wind-banner touches forward;
with the palms facing upward, one recites the mantra and,
by means of the mudrā, causes all the deities to arise from below.
This is called the mudrā for generating [the deity].
Next, one invites the principal deity and others.
The mantra and mudrā for the invocation are as follows:
Oṃ vajrasamaya jaḥ jaḥ. As for the form of the mudrā: interlace the wisdom and samādhi fingers to form a vajra-fist.
Not understanding this fist,
one uses the wind-wheel of wisdom to strike the great emptiness of wisdom;
the hand of meditative concentration does likewise.
Thus, these three plucks constitute the rite for inviting the honored deities.
One should visualize a multi-storied pavilion erected at the location where the principal deity resides,
and imagine that within this pavilion there is a precious lotus flower.
Looking upward at the great perfect luminosity,
there are nine wheels within;
in each wheel of the Vajradhātu path, the principal deity is seated.
The diagram is as follows on the left.
Within the great luminous circle, it is divided into nine circles and eight precious vases.
Twelve vajras and four jewel wheels;
from the mouths of eight precious vases, eight vajras stand upright.
It rests upon four vajra-wheels;
from the four sides of the wheels, four vajras extend horizontally.
Each vase and each vajra is further adorned with colored silk ribbons.
Within the vast, luminous expanse of dense, hanging clouds,
each sits upon a throne for the nine holy ones;
at the center is the Great Vairocana Tathāgata.
He wears a jeweled crown of the five wisdoms and sits upon a throne supported by seven lions,
seated in the full lotus posture and forming the Dharma-realm mudrā.
The remaining deities are fully explained in the chapter on the lower maṇḍala.
The mantra for invitation is as follows:
Oṃ vajra-kuśa jaḥ. As for the form of its mudrā:
employ the Trailokyavijaya mudrā;
raise the two vāyu-maṇḍalas (the index fingers) to form the shape of a hook.
Moving the hook constitutes the formal invitation.
Once they have graciously accepted the invitation and arrived, one should next invite them to enter the recitation mandala. The mantra for the invitation to enter is as follows:
Oṃ vajrapāśa hūṃ. As for the form of its mudrā:
with the two vajra-fists, extend the two earth-wheels (the thumbs) and interlace the two space-wheels (the index fingers), inserting them into the palms.
The right hand presses down upon the left.
Having been invited to enter, they abide according to the invitation, performing the samaya.
The mantra for requesting him to remain is:
Oṃ vajra-kaṇṭha āḥ. As for the mudrā: form a vajra-fist and extend the two earth-touching fingers (tarjanīs).
Interlace the two wheels of emptiness, bringing them into the palms with the right pressing upon the left;
this serves to invite [the deities] up to the stage of joy,
thereby causing them to become firm and stable.
Then recite the mantra.
The mantra for firmness is:
Oṃ sarvatathāgatābhiṣekavajrādhiṣṭhāna. As for the characteristics of its hand-seal (mudrā):
When wisdom and concentration strike one another, they become firm and stable.
Next, one should perform the ritual ablution for both the deity and oneself.
The mantra for the consecration is as follows:
Oṃ vajranogaṭa. As for the mudrā of this [mantra]:
join the tips of the space-fingers (the thumbs) of the two wisdom-hands;
keep the remaining fingers extended and press them together while reciting over the water vessel.
Visualize bathing the Honored One;
sprinkle the mudrā upon the crown of your own head and offer argha water.
Visualize that [the nectar] is poured upon the crown of the Honored One’s head.
Also, using this mudrā, prostrate and recite the mantra seven times. 4.

Chapter on the Cultivation of Yoga and the Offering of Incense and Flowers: The Mantra of the Uṣṇīṣavijaya Buddha-Crown. Chapter Four: The Cultivation of Yoga and the Offering of Incense, Flowers, Food, Drink, Lamps, and so forth. Offer incense, flowers, food, drink, lamps, and other such items for the fourth time.
Recite and maintain the root mantra to offer it as an oblation.
First, the mantra for offering incense is:
Oṃ vajra-dhūpe svāhā. As for the mudrā of this hand gesture:
Forming the Vajra Fist, press it upon the incense and recite the mantra seventeen times. Thereupon,
it becomes a true precious incense that pervades the ten directions, the void, and the Dharma-realm.
Next, the mantra for the offering of flowers is:
Oṃ vajra puṣpe. As for the mudrā: join the palms of the vajra hands and perform the empowerment with this seal.
Recite the mantra one hundred and seven times;
it will then become a true jewel-flower and so forth.
Next, offer the jewel-lamp with its mantra and mudrā.
The mantra is:
Oṃ vajra-dhiti svāhā. As for the form of its mudrā:
form a vajra-fist.
Place the two thumbs upright in the space above the heart;
recite the mantra seven times,
and it will become a jewel lamp that pervades the entire realm of empty space.
Next, the mantra for offering the fragrant unguent is:
Oṃ vajragandhe. As for its mudrā: with the hands of wisdom and concentration palms facing downward, extend the fingers like spokes.
Seal the wheel of emptiness with the great emptiness of wisdom.
Recite the mantra seventeen times.
Next, one should take refuge in the Triple Gem, confess transgressions, rejoice in merit, and make requests for merit.
Constantly resolve to attain bodhicitta, praise the virtues of the Buddha, and make supreme vows.
Those who take refuge in the Triple Gem vow that from this present body until they sit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), [they shall remain steadfast].
I take refuge in the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed three bodies;
I take refuge in the Dharma-treasury of the Vaipulya Mahāyāna;
I take refuge in the Saṃgha of all non-retrogressive Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
One should take refuge in the Triple Gem in this manner.
Next, regarding the confession of transgressions:
from beginningless time until the present moment.
Afflictions have long shrouded the source, causing the flow of birth and death;
through the three types of karmic obstructions, boundless transgressions have been committed.
Today, with a sincere heart, I reveal and repent of them all.
One should simply engage in extensive repentance so that one's transgressions may be eliminated.
Next, regarding the arousal of the bodhicitta:
from this very day until one sits at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), [one should maintain this resolve].
I vow to give rise to the unsurpassed mind of great bodhicitta;
I vow to deliver immeasurable classes of sentient beings, wishing that they all be freed from the great suffering of birth and death.
This mind now generated shall further remain free from the two marks of self and phenomena.
Because my Dharma is equal and devoid of intrinsic nature,
one should thus generate the bodhicitta and empower it with mantras.
To cause the bodhicitta to become firm and non-regressive, the mantra is:
Oṃ bodhicitta-mutpādayāmi. As for the mudrā of this [mantra]:
Joining the vajra palms, generate the bodhicitta and recite the mantra seventeen times.
As for rejoicing in the merit:
The Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time have fully cultivated immeasurable merit for the sake of sentient beings;
may I rejoice in all such merit.
Regarding the exhortation to remain forever:
I pray that all Buddhas may long abide in the world,
relying on the principle of yoga for the sake of non-abiding nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, they requested that the Great Dharma Wheel be turned throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Those who made these supreme vows prayed:
"May all sentient beings abound in wealth and treasures."
One should always courageously practice giving and be fully endowed with wisdom;
one should always maintain great patience and delight in creating virtuous conditions;
and having attained the knowledge of past lives, one should compassionately regard all sentient beings.
May all sentient beings, in whatever place they are born,
always obtain such various superior things.
Next, direct the mind to make offerings.
Mentally visualizing this,
one imagines that all flowers of the water and land— unowned by anyone—
fill the entirety of space throughout the ten directions.

Furthermore, there were oceans of clouds of exquisite human and celestial unguents, incense, lamps, banners, and pennants; various kinds of drums, music, songs, and dances; and singing by female performers, along with nets of pearls and various jeweled bells suspended [therein].
The heavens were adorned with clouds of flower garlands, exquisite white whisks,
subtle bells and chimes, jeweled cords, lattices, wish-fulfilling jewel trees, and garments;
they were further graced by celestial kitchens of most sublime fragrant soups and palaces and towers embellished with precious pillars.
All ornaments for the body, such as crowns and necklaces, and so forth—
the yogin should direct his mind to pervade the entirety of space;
making offerings with such a heart of utmost sincerity is the most supreme and excellent.
Therefore, the practitioner, with a resolute mind,
practices this dharma by directing the mind toward making offerings,
reciting and upholding mantras, and performing mudrās.
Whatever one has visualized above shall all be accomplished.
The mantra for directing the mind is as follows:
Oṃ sarvathā khaṃ uttare saparāhima-aṃ gagaṇe jñaṃ svāhā. Recite this mantra seven times.
This constitutes the ordinary offering.
As for the mudrā:
join the vajra-palms and place them upon the crown of the head.
Recite this mantra seven times,
and the various implements for offering will immediately be accomplished.
Next, protect the five parts of the body with the mantra and mudrā.
The mantra is:
Oṃ citta-pratītya-vaśena kārumi. By reciting this mantra, one causes all Tathāgatas to abide in the perfect samaya.
One will be able to accomplish all the activities of the Buddhas and swiftly attain fulfillment.
Chapter Five: Cultivating Yoga and the Five Wisdoms, the Section on the Supreme Mantra. Furthermore, regarding the practitioner of yoga (*yogin*):
Because one abides in the sublime bodhicitta oneself,
one swiftly enters the wisdom-mind that contemplates bodhicitta.
The mantra for contemplating bodhicitta is as follows:
Oṃ bodhicittam utpādayāmi. This is called the mantra for generating the bodhicitta;
it is also called the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (ādarśajñāna).
It causes one to swiftly give rise to the bodhicitta;
at the very moment of first generating that mind, one attains perfect enlightenment,
which is precisely the meaning of the Dharmakāya.
Next, the mantra of the Wisdom of Equality is taught as follows:
Oṃ tiṣṭha vajra. By reciting this mantra, the mind is swiftly made to abide and prevented from becoming distracted.
This is the meaning of the *saṃbhogakāya*.
Next, the mantra of the *kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna* is spoken:
OṂ ĀTĀḤ SARVA-TATHĀGATA-SATYA-HŪṂ. Fourth, the mantra of the *pratyavekṣaṇājñāna* is spoken:
Oṃ svabhāva-śuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ. This is named the wisdom of wondrous observation (pratyavekṣaṇājñāna).
It signifies the meaning of the saṃbhogakāya, and it also signifies the dharmakāya of subsequently attained wisdom (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna).
Next, the mantra for the Wisdom of Ultimate Skillful Means is spoken:
Oṃ sarva-tathāgata-mūrdha-svabhāva-ātmako ’ham. This is named the Wisdom of Ultimate Skillful Means.
Regarding the meaning of the nirmāṇakāya:
in the gate of progressive cultivation, taking skillful means as the ultimate constitutes the meaning of the dharmakāya of subsequently attained wisdom.
This clarifies that they are to be placed within the five directions of the central womb.
As for the mudrās of the mantras of the five wisdoms:
with the two hands of wisdom and concentration joined in an outer *vajra-śṛṅkhalā* (crossed) gesture.
Join the palms into fists;
extend the two fire-wheels (index fingers) straight upward,
and join the two earth-wheels (thumbs) together.
The two *vāyu-maṇḍalas* (wind wheels) are bent and each rests upon the back joints of the two *tejo-maṇḍalas* (fire wheels),
at a distance of about two or three finger-widths [from them].
The two *mahākha-maṇḍalas* (great space wheels) stand side by side vertically.
Its form is like a five-pronged vajra.
By means of this single mudrā, one universally employs the five wisdoms.
Subsequently, one uses the Mahāvairocana Dharmadhātu Mudrā to consecrate the five locations.
One immediately becomes possessed of the body of the fivefold Dharma-body and the myriad virtues.
As for the mudrā of the Dharmadhātu:
with the wisdom of skillful means, each forms a vajra-fist.
The hand of wisdom grasps the wind-banner of skillful means and empowers the five locations,
then abides upon the heart.
One’s own body becomes the body of the Tathāgata Vairocana.
The jeweled crown upon his head contains the five wisdom Buddhas;
these are the Five Cakravartins,
who embody the meaning of the five wisdoms.
Then, one should empower the five places with the heart-mantra of the Sarvabuddhoṣṇīṣacakravartin.
The heart-mantra of the Sarvabuddhoṣṇīṣacakravartin is as follows:
Oṃ dhu ru hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. As for the characteristics of its hand-seal (mudrā):
Interlace the two hands within each other to form fists;
extend the two middle wheels (middle fingers) straight upward—this is it.
This mudrā and its mantra are applicable for all purposes and accomplish all tasks.
This is for summoning, dispatching, binding the boundary, and protecting the body; it is universally applicable in all instances.
Next, regarding the mantra of the deity, the description of its mudrā is as follows: cross the two hands with the palms facing outward.
Joining the palms into fists, bend the right fingers into hooks and form the wind-banner mudrā;
this is used for empowerment at the five locations during rites of augmentation.
Alternatively, one may use a single hand for the rite of summoning;
furthermore, as described in the sūtras, one joins the palms with both hands and presses the right thumb over the left thumb.
This is used for the time of averting calamities.
When performing recitation for subjugation,
it is done by placing the left hand over the right.
Then, holding the rosary and joining the palms above the crown of the head,
one should hold the rosary at the heart and perform the recitation.
One should recite each [mantra] in accordance with its respective root ritual (*mūlavidhi*).
One will swiftly attain the fulfillment of one's desired aspirations,
provided that there is no lack of sincerity or engagement in evil deeds,
which would instead lead to self-harm.
Chapter Six: The Cultivation of the Mantra of the Yoga-Deity Uṣṇīṣavijaya. Furthermore, I shall now briefly explain the method for cultivating the mantra of the yoga-deity.
Recite this yourself on the fifteenth day of each month,

the practitioner should construct a small altar beside a dragon’s pool or spring.
One should fashion eight stakes from mulberry wood and place them within the altar.
Furthermore, take three bowls of milk and curd and place them upon the altar as well.
Recite the empowerment mantra over the wooden stakes and other items one hundred and eight times.
Then, drive the wooden stakes into the four sides and eight locations around the spring.
Furthermore, one should pour milk and curd into the pool.
Moreover, one should empower golden leaf-shards,
place them upon lotus leaves, and set them within the spring.
The practitioner says aloud:
"Good friend, you are now in peril;
you have been bound by various non-Buddhist practitioners."
Now that this ritual procedure is completed,
I shall protect you with the dhāraṇī and dismiss you.
Take these lotus leaves and the mantra, and enter the water.
If the practitioner recites the *hā* syllable three times,
the prohibitory spells of the non-Buddhists will be immediately destroyed,
and that nāga will attain liberation without further difficulty.
The dragon immediately emerged to make offerings to the practitioner.
The dragon’s mouth asked,
"Master Cao, what are your instructions?"
The practitioner says aloud:
"You may, at all times according to the season, raise clouds and bring forth rain.
Place this dhāraṇī upon the crown of your head."
May you all forever be free from calamity.
As for the thirty-fourth dharma:
if there should be a great flood that overflows and causes harm to people, [this dharma shall protect them].

The Practice of Yoga for Painting Images. Regarding the *Uṣṇīṣavijaya-dhāraṇī*, this is the seventh chapter on the practice of yoga for painting images. Furthermore, I shall now further explain the practice of yoga for swiftly attaining the *siddhis* with and without signs.
The precedents differ for internal and external [practices].
Regarding the method for external images,
one must first paint the image.
Select an auspicious, virtuous, and favorable month, season, and day.
Rise at dawn and draw [the mandala].
Regarding the "favorable month":
The first, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, twelfth,
and other such months are considered the most excellent months.
As for the auspicious days:
During solar and lunar eclipses, at times of earthquakes, and on the day of the constellation Ārdrā—
these are considered the most excellent and superior days.
Alternatively, one may take the fifteenth day of the waxing moon.
Alternatively, one may select the twenty-third day or other such dates;
having thus chosen the day, month, season, and time,
one summons the painters and bathes them.
He confers the samaya precepts or the samaya initiation;
at each instance of entering or exiting [the ritual space], he bathes and changes his robes.
One should consume the three white foods and avoid impure food, among other things;
furthermore, no price shall be paid for them.
As for the materials for the painting, they are white woolen cloth.
Alternatively, one may paint it according to the dharma upon fine cotton cloth, silk, or similar materials,
strictly following the diagram shown below.
Regarding the cloth, silk, or wool upon which it is painted,
the dimensions may be as one desires;
at the center.
Paint a large, brilliant white circle.
Furthermore, divide this large, brilliant circle into nine circles,
and place jeweled vases in the eight directions.
Insert famous flowers into the mouth of the vase;
upon it, place a three-pronged vajra.
At its center is a circle, with four precious wheels placed at the four corners of the exterior.
All [the vajras] are joined together;
the necks of the precious vases and the vajras are bound with silk ribbons that hang down.
In the center, within a circle, is painted Vairocana Tathāgata,
wearing a crown of five Buddhas and adorned with the radiant light of various jewel flowers.
He sits cross-legged upon seven lion thrones,
his hands forming the Dharma-realm mudrā;
within the circular brilliance of his left hand, he depicts the White Parasol Buddha-uṣṇīṣa Cakravartin.
He wears a crown of the five wisdoms;
his left hand holds a lotus,
upon which is placed a white parasol.
With his right hand raised in the gesture of the open palm, he sits in the half-lotus posture.
The radiance of his body and the halo around his head are shaped like five-colored wheels.
Within the aforementioned circular brilliance, one should depict the Most Victorious Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Cakravartin,
wearing a crown of five wisdoms and adorned with various ornaments,
with a halo behind his head and a light radiating from his entire body.
It resembles a chariot wheel and is endowed with various colors.
In his right hand he holds a lotus flower, upon which rests a precious wheel with eight spokes.
It is possessed of various colors, and its radiant flames encircle it in a circle.
Seated in the full lotus posture upon a lotus flower,
with the left hand palm upturned,
one should paint Uṣṇīṣavijayā in front of the central radiant orb.
He is also named the Buddha-Cūḍāmaṇi Wheel-Turning King who Removes Obstructions.
He sits cross-legged upon a lotus pedestal, his complexion white,
with both hands below the navel as if entering meditative absorption.
In his palms he holds a lotus flower;
upon the lotus is a vajra hook,
as in the case of the Uṣṇīṣacakravartin and others.
Adorned with various radiances and the five-wisdom crowns,
they all sit in the full-lotus posture upon white lotus seats, according to the Yoga-tantra diagrams.
Within the circle behind Mahāvairocana Tathāgata, one should paint the Radiant Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa,
also known as the Uṣṇīṣacakravartin of the Mass of Light;
his left hand holds a lotus flower.
Upon the flower pedestal, draw the seal (mudrā) of the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa.
From atop the uṣṇīṣa, light rays radiate forth,
as do the lights from the five-wisdom jewel crown.
As previously described,
he raises his right hand with the palm facing upward,
to the left side of the Uṣṇīṣavijayā Buddha-crown.
Within the circle of radiant clarity, draw the Victorious Uṣṇīṣa Buddha;
his left hand holds a sword,
and his right hand raises its palm.
Adorned with the various ornaments of the five-buddha crown,
the wheel-light is also as described above.
To the right of that Uṣṇīṣavijayā Buddha-Usnīṣa...
Paint the Buddha King of the Uṣṇīṣa;
his right hand holds a vajra,
and his left hand has its palm raised.
The five-wisdom crown,
the wheel-light flames, the necklaces, and so forth,
are all modeled after the examples of the aforementioned deities.
Within the circular brilliance on the right side of the *Prabhaketurāja* (Light-Cluster Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa), one should paint the *Anantasvararāja* (Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa King of Infinite Sound).
His right hand holds a lotus flower,
and upon the center of the lotus pedestal, one should paint the letter *ŚAṂ*.
The left hand is raised above the breast with the palm facing upward.
He wears a five-buddha crown and is adorned with the radiance of a wheel, and so forth.
Adorned with various ornaments as desired,
within a circular brilliance on the left side of the mass of light, one should paint the Buddha-uṣṇīṣarāja in his manifest form,
holding an opened lotus flower in his left hand.
With his right hand [resting on his knee] and his right knee raised, he sits in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*).
His wheel-light and jeweled necklaces are as described above;
all [deities] possess the marks of great benevolence and compassion.
On the lower left side, paint the deity Trailokyavijaya.
He stands in a diagonal, striding posture upon a half-moon discus;
he is blue in color, with fangs protruding from his upper lip.
He has four hands:
two hands form the samaya-mudrā,
and one hand forms the heart-mudrā.
Holding a vajra bound in one hand,
to the right, within a red triangular radiance, draw the Lord Acala,
seated in the half-lotus posture upon a flat rock.
One eye blazed with wrath while the other was closed; he bit his lower lip.
One side of his body was turned backward, and his crimson hair, matted and interlocked, hung down toward his left.
His body is further plump and full, like the form of a youth;
his right hand holds a sword and his left hand grasps a lasso.
Between the two vidyārājas, the practitioner of yoga sits.
In front of the incense burner,
the image above is painted with a jeweled canopy;
on both sides are painted six figures of Śuddhāvāsa deva-boys riding upon clouds.
The upper halves of their bodies emerge, each holding incense, flowers, jeweled garlands, and so forth.
This is based on the aforementioned illustration,
or according to the method for visualizing the external forms.
The practitioner of yoga contemplates his own body as the Dharmakāya of Vairocana,
pervading the entire Dharma-realm and being of one and the same essential nature.
There are no other characteristics.
I have now finished briefly explaining the methods for visualizing the image and drawing it.
For anyone who wishes to perform the ritual and receive the *Buddhottama-śikhara-vidyā-mantra*, [the following should be observed].
First, one must paint an image.
As for the method of painting the image:
take high-quality silk.
Alternatively, use white cotton cloth or silk measuring three spans in width and ten feet in height;
do not use animal glue among the pigments.
One must use fragrant resin.
The painter must be pure and abstain from pungent spices.
Beginning from the first day of the dark fortnight,
the painted image must be completed within seven days.
One should depict Mount Amṛta.
Within the mountain, he fashioned various groves of trees, flowers, fruits, flowing springs, birds, and beasts; in the mountain,
he fashioned a meditation cave, and within the cave,
he fashioned Śākyamuni Buddha sitting in the full lotus posture.
To the right of the Buddha is Śakra, Lord of Devas,
surrounded by his entire retinue;
to the left is a son of the Gandharvas.
His name was Śubhavyūha;
his appearance was dignified and majestic like that of a bodhisattva,
and his hair, garments, and crown were likewise so.
He is adorned with various necklaces and flower crowns;
furthermore, a white cotton cloth is draped diagonally over his left shoulder, and he holds a ball-staff in his right hand. He is also accompanied by a retinue of gandharvas.
They surround the Well-Situated One, performing songs, dances, and music.
To the left and right of the Buddha, respectively, are depicted two sets of the Four Great Heavenly Kings along with their retinues.
Furthermore, on the Buddha’s left side, Mahābrahmā and Māra are depicted.
Once the painted image has been completed,
one must immediately construct an altar and receive the dharma.
As for the method of constructing the altar:
First, seek out a pure site where there are no shards or stones.
Mix five kinds of fragrant water with clean earth to form mud,
and smear this mud over a square area of one *zhang*.
Furthermore, construct a square and circular area at the center of the mandala measuring one cubit (hasta) in diameter; within this, fashion a single *uṣṇīṣa*.
On the four sides outside the mandala, place offerings of food and drink in each direction.
There were seven basins set out individually;
in each of the four directions, a set of incense burners was placed,
and various famous incenses were burned.
Place a copper flask at the southern gate;
fill the flask with scented water and install it at the seat of Śakra.
At the eastern gate, the son of the gandharva Sthira should be seated;
at the western gate, the mantra-practitioner himself shall sit,
facing eastward.
The Buddha image faces west.
Furthermore, banners made of five-colored silk cloth are suspended on the four sides outside the ritual arena.
Furthermore, place five lamps:
one lamp is to be set in the center at a high position,
and four lamps are to be placed in the four corners below.
It is shaped like a stupa;
within the mandala, various kinds of flowers and offering articles are scattered.
Place them outside the mandala on its four sides;
do not place them inside the mandala.
Recite the mantra within the site of practice for seven days.
Once the recitation has been completed for ten thousand full repetitions,
the Buddha’s crown will emit a great radiance;
within seven days, the mantra-practitioner [shall attain the desired result].
You must repeatedly confess and repent, give rise to great compassion, and make vast vows never to regress.
At that moment, you will know that the Dharma is accomplished;
do not harbor any further doubt.

perform the homa three times each,
following the procedure as described above.
All the *mus* wood and other materials are to be offered as *homa*.
The incense and other substances for offering are to be mixed together with a porridge made of the five grains.

First, perform the homa ritual three times each for the sovereign, the queen, the crown prince, the various princes and princesses, the ministers and officials, all sentient beings of the dharma realm,
and even for one's own body.
Finally, take the trays of rice, fruits, and other offerings from the four sides of the hearth and perform consecration and homa for each one.
At the four corners of the fire altar...
Place five precious vases, incense burners, fruit trays, and so forth,
according to the ritual of the Great Maṇḍala.
Construct fire pits that are square, circular, triangular, or crescent-shaped.
First, rely upon the ritual procedures of the aforementioned Great Maṇḍala;
if one can perform the rites in this manner, there shall be nothing that is not accomplished.
As for those of evil signs:
During the performance of the *homā*,
the fire should suddenly go out,
or black flames may appear, or sounds such as those of donkeys and mules may be heard.
These are all signs of failure.
If the color of the fire corresponds with the original rite, it is a sign of success;
the same applies to its sound or appearance.
This is the characteristic of failure when the rite is not in accordance with its intended purpose.
If it is a rite for averting calamities, the color of the fire is white;
if it is a rite for increase, the color of the fire is yellow.
If it is a rite of subjugation (*abhicāra*), the color of the fire is red;
if it is a rite of summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*), the color of the fire is blue.
As for its appearance, it is like a parasol, a *vajra*, a lotus, and a bell.
The radiant light and the excellent,
sublime voice are both in accord with the fundamental dharma and are signs of accomplishment.
Whenever one performs the practices of recitation or homa, [these signs will appear].
If one practices according to the primary time,
one will swiftly attain *siddhi*.
That is to say, from the first watch through the second and third watches of the night is the time for the removal of calamities.
At midnight is the time for summoning;
from the latter part of the night until dawn is the time for increasing;
at midday is the time for subjugating.
Regarding these four types of homa,
each has its own distinct varieties of wood, incense, medicinal herbs, hearth-shapes,
and other such details.
This should be performed according to the *Susiddhikara*,
adapting it as appropriate for the occasion.
Thus has been explained the ritual procedure for the *homa* of material substances.
The second is the internal homa.
The three locations are of one essence.
Regarding "the three locations are of one essence":
The Great Maṇḍala is itself the homa maṇḍala;
it is the homa maṇḍala.
This is one's own body;
one's own body is the Fire God (Agni);
the Fire God is Vairocana Tathāgata.
Vairocana Tathāgata,
the Fire Deity,
his own body.
The three types [of bodies] are non-dual and without distinction;
because they are of one essence, they are fully endowed with the three bodies.
Mahāvairocana pervades and illuminates the entire dharma-realm.
There is nowhere it does not pervade.
It is neither arising nor ceasing, transcending both speech and thought.
Whether in arising or non-arising, there is nothing that is not Mahāvairocana.
Therefore, it is designated as the Dharmakāya.
As for *homa*, in this region it is [the ritual] of the Fire Deity (*Agnideva*).
Fire can burn away grasses, trees, shrubs, and forests without exception;
"heaven" refers to wisdom.
The fire of wisdom can burn away all stumps and remnants of ignorance, leaving nothing unburnt.
Vairocana Mahāvairocana is the Dharmakāya;
the wisdom-fire of the deity Agni is the Sambhogakāya;
and one’s own ability to abide in skillful means is the Nirmāṇakāya.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Skillful means are the ultimate;
they are capable of performing all Buddha-works."
Therefore, one's own body becomes the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
These three types [of bodies] are of a single essence and enter into the wheel of the five wisdoms (*pañcajñānacakra*).
One visualizes above the crown of the head the arising of the fire of wisdom from the *dharmadhātu*, which incinerates all karmic obstructions and the like.
It can fulfill all the vows of sentient beings.
The four types of homa are performed according to their respective root rituals;
for the removal of calamities and so forth, they follow exclusively the external homa.
It is able to transform all obstacles and cause various merits and virtues to arise;
it is employed according to the sequence of the twelve kinds of fire rituals from the Vairocana Sūtra.
Chapter Eleven: The Method for Cultivating Yoga to Invoke Rain. Regarding the method for cultivating yoga to invoke rain through the Uṣṇīṣavijaya Dhāraṇī, I shall now explain it in sequence.
For the benefit of all beings,
I shall briefly explain the method for praying for rain.
When the weather is parched with drought and the sweet rains do not fall in due season.
A scorching drought extends for a thousand li, causing the crops to wither and fail to grow.
All living beings are filled with dread, and the land is not at peace;
calamities of fire arise one after another.
The lives of sentient beings, both aquatic and terrestrial,
depend upon morning and evening for their sustenance.
When a practitioner of Yoga perceives such beings undergoing suffering, they give rise to a mind of great compassion.
Thereupon, he briefly constructed a rain-prayer maṇḍala.
As for the dimensions of this rain-prayer maṇḍala,
they were to be determined according to the occasion as appropriate.
The base of the altar is one chi high;
the ground is smeared with pure clay mixed with cow dung,
and this is further extended beyond the altar.
On a clean patch of ground measuring four or five chi,
apply a coating of clay and various blended fragrant powders mixed with water,
spreading it on very thinly.
Extending downward for three feet to a clean area,
the maṇḍala shall be one foot high,
with walkways established at its four gates.
The foundation was further raised by one or two cubits (hasta).
Along its perimeter, the eight great nāga kings together with their queens and retinues were depicted.
The one in the east had three heads and a body three cubits long.
In the south, there are five heads and the body is five cubits long;
in the west, seven heads and the body is seven cubits long;
in the north, eight heads and the body is eight cubits long.
The central [deity] has nine heads and a body nine cubits tall;
his consorts likewise correspond to the king,
each leading their own retinue.
"One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight," and so forth;
various bodily forms are similar to these, for which there are illustrative diagrams below.
The aforementioned rain-praying maṇḍala varies in its dimensions.
If it is for a state, it should be thirty-eight cubits square;
if for a commandery or district, fifteen cubits square;
and if for a ward, village, or town, eight cubits square.
If there is no formal invitation from a patron,
one may perform the rite for the sake of all sentient beings of the dharma-realm out of one's own initiative,
whether staying in a mountain forest or an araṇya.
For those who perform recitation in temples, monasteries, settlements, villages, or towns,
[the area] should be four cubits or two cubits wide,
according to the size appropriate for the occasion.
This maṇḍala is divided into three enclosures.
The central great circle is further divided into five circles,
and each of these circles is again divided into five circles.
In the center is painted the Honored One, Uṣṇīṣavijayā Cakravartin, mounted upon a king of golden-winged garuḍas as his seat.
With wings spread and in a wrathful posture, he raises one foot in the gesture of seizing the frontal lobes of the various dragon heads.
The nāgas and others all join their palms and bow their heads;
the principal deity grasps a vajra-hook and assumes a threatening posture, facing forward.
In each of the four circles, draw the Buddha-Usnīṣa Sitātapatrā and others as the center of five circles;
on each of the four sides, draw the four Pāramitās and others,
all seated upon the king of garuḍas as their thrones.
The configuration resembles the layout of the central court.
It depicts the manner of lifting the feet to tread upon the dragon kings and others,
with four seals pressed upon the tails of the dragons and so forth.
In the four corners of the outer courtyard are the four offerings.
On the eastern and western sides, paint a Buddha together with two bodhisattvas;
on the left and right, paint Aparājita-rāja and the wrathful king Durjaya.
In the center of the northern face, paint the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvararāja;
to his left and right, [paint] the Mother Goddesses, the Family Heart Deities, the Vidyārājas, and the Vidyārāja Sumbha-Hayagrīva.
Facing south are the Lord of Secrets, Vajrapāṇi, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha-rāja,
the Mother Deities of the left and right sections, the Heart Deities of the sections,
the Bodhisattva Krodhavajra, the Wrathful Great Vidyārājas, and others.
On the north and south sides of the western gate,
paint the Vajrahūṃkāra and Acalanātha Vidyārājas respectively.
In the outer enclosure, paint the protective deities of the ten directions for each respective quarter, together with their retinues and four attendants.
On the east and west sides of the southern gate,
paint the Sun Deity and the Moon Deity together with their consorts;
in the empty spaces on all four sides [likewise].
In each [of the four directions], paint the seven luminaries and the twenty-eight lunar mansions, each holding their respective hand-seals (*mudrā*).
In a secluded area on one side, paint the various *siddhi*-attaining immortals (*ṛṣi*),
each with their own attendants.
The great bodhisattvas along with their attendants shall be installed exactly according to the diagram.
These thirty-eight cubits shall be executed by the craftsmen of the kingdom.
Having submitted this to the prefectures and counties, [paintings] of fifteen cubits shall be produced;
those of eight cubits shall be painted according to the same upper [specifications],
or else within the central area.
The Five Peaks, the Four Great Rivers, the Dragons of the Five Directions,
and so forth, are further painted as a surrounding encirclement on the outermost edge of the maṇḍala.
Once the painting is completed:
In all the inner and outer courtyards, various kinds of food and drink are set out,
exactly as in the offerings of incense, flowers, and so forth at the great maṇḍala.
As for those [measures] of four cubits and two cubits:
It is not necessary to paint a formal image according to the ritual rules;
it is sufficient to draw a mudrā, or simply write a seed-syllable (*bīja*), or write the name.
At a spot two feet away from the outside of the maṇḍala, on a level and clean surface.
Grind the leaves of the *nimba* tree to extract the juice and smear it everywhere with blue pigment.
On each of the four sides, paint a great Nāgarāja together with his attendants and so forth;
furthermore, paint their respective consorts along with their retinues.
Those with three heads, five heads, seven, eight, or nine heads, and so forth,
are each to be drawn according to their respective original directions.
From within the path at the western gate, they emerge with only half their bodies visible.
The Central Dragon King, together with his queen and retinue,
reverently makes offerings to the various Honored Ones, subdues [obstacles], and requests the descent of sweet rain.
As for those measuring thirty-eight cubits or more, up to fifteen cubits:
There are twenty-five precious vases;
for those measuring eight cubits or less,
five vases will suffice.
The vessel should be made of blue-glazed porcelain or new earthenware. Every day,
one should add fresh water along with blue pigment (qīngdài), the five treasures, and the five grains.
Insert bamboo branches, cypress leaves, and the like into the mouth;
tie a length of blue silk, seven or eight feet long, around the neck;
and spread a blue canopy over the altar.
Hang banners on all four sides, forty-nine in total, each the size of a person;
hang a forty-nine-foot blue banner directly to the east of the altar.
[Prepare] various foods, drinks, incense, flowers, and so forth.
Just as with the great maṇḍala,
three or five cubits outside the western side of the maṇḍala, one should construct a homa altar consisting of one hearth;
it may possess four types of hearth shapes.
Furthermore, write seed-syllables in each of the four directions within the hearth.
As for these seed-syllables:
the syllable *A* (𑀅), square-shaped and yellow, is in the east.
The syllable *Ha* is blue in color, located in the west, and has a crescent shape.
The syllable *Vaṃ* is white in color, located in the north, and is circular in shape.
The syllable *Laṃ* is red in color, located in the south, and is triangular in shape.
At the base of each, draw mudrās and so forth;
in the east, draw a wheel;
in the north, a lotus.
The vajra of the south and the hook of the west should be drawn according to their respective original directions,
or they may be fashioned separately within their own respective quarters.
Invoke the fire deity as the principal object of worship (iṣṭadevatā), along with the various vidyārājas and others.

Proceed entirely according to the aforementioned homa rules without any variation; however, on the first day, perform the rite for averting calamities, and on the second day, the rite for increasing prosperity.
On the third day, perform the summoning;
on the fourth and fifth days, the subjugation;
and on the sixth and seventh days, the subjugation through extreme wrath and so forth.
If, on the appointed day, sweet rain falls,
one should immediately cease [the ritual] and perform homas for the purpose of pacifying calamities, increasing prosperity,
and so forth, for the sake of the nāgas and others.
At the time of subjugation, use a wooden staff made of *kashi* wood with both ends sharpened to touch fire;
take thorns from the *kaṇṭaka* tree.
Perform the homa by anointing both ends with black mustard oil; or,
fashion the shape of a nāga using wax mixed with the powder of white and black mustard seeds, poisons, and so forth,
and perform the homa by cutting it into inch-long segments.
Upon obtaining rain, one should perform acts such as offering prayers for joy and so forth.
Furthermore, there is a method wherein one takes a piece of silk and inscribes the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-dhāraṇī* in Sanskrit characters;
on its four sides, one should draw various mudrās.
If one performs the empowerment through recitation and casts [the substances] into a dragon pond,
rain will immediately fall.
If there is a kingdom...
Droughts and floods were out of season;
yin and yang were not in harmony;
and parched lands extended for a thousand li.
Where there is no green grass, crops, or the like,
they may turn their backs on kindness and virtue, give rise to rebellious intent,
and slaughter immeasurable sentient beings.
Seeing such things,
the wise person will certainly give rise to a mind of great loving-kindness and great compassion and perform the rite of subjugation;
this is due to the power of their vow of great compassion.
Those people will both be reborn in heaven and shall not incur any transgressions;
first, however, one must eliminate obstacles for the sake of the state.
Recite the Uṣṇīṣavijayā Dhāraṇī one thousand or ten thousand times.
If acting as a minister or aide,
recite it five hundred times.
If for the sake of all common people,
recite it ten thousand times;
if for the sake of all sentient beings in the dharma realm.
Recite it one thousand times.
Then, perform the homa rites for subjugation and so forth, each according to the preceding instructions;
thus, one’s intentions will be fulfilled.
Furthermore, there is a method: perform homa and recitation at the four periods of each day.
Consecrate white mustard seeds and strike them upon the heart of the Dragon King one thousand and eight times every day.
One will then achieve one's purpose.
Alternatively, one may visualize oneself as the body of the Buddha Uṣṇīṣavijayā,
riding upon the king of the golden-winged garuḍas.
The wrathful one soars upward,
intending to trample upon the dragon’s form with a vajra hook.
By assuming the posture of a hooking gesture,
one will immediately obtain sweet rain;
alternatively, one may recite the mantra while striking various nāgas with white mustard seeds.
Alternatively, mix white mustard seeds, asafoetida, and red mustard oil,
and perform one thousand or one hundred and eight *homa* offerings.
Or else, simply perform *homa* offerings in sequence for all the vidyārājas within the maṇḍala.
Append the words for subjugation to all of them.
By performing the ritual in this manner,
rain will immediately fall.
Then, having performed the *homa* rites for the removal of calamities, the increase of merit,
and so forth, he further conferred empowerment upon the various nāga kings and others,
making extensive offerings to inspire their joy.
He further provided food and drink,
extensively arranging offerings;
all the food and drink were placed within lotus leaves.
Send it into the river water or into a dragon pool; then,
bury the five-colored silks directly in front [of the site].
The offerings made by that Buddha, his bodhisattvas,
and others shall be disposed of according to the ritual;
this is when the rite is correctly performed.
One should wear blue garments,
or otherwise wear clothing appropriate to each respective direction.
On the homa altar, five vases should be placed.
All offerings of food and drink follow the ritual of the Great Maṇḍala without exception;
if one does not rely on this,
the rite will not be accomplished.
Thereafter, when turning back the challenges and making requests,
one must perform them according to the Dharma;
then one will swiftly attain accomplishment.

Chapter Twelve: Entering the Sphere of Accomplishment. Regarding the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā Dhāraṇī*, this is the twelfth chapter, "Entering the Sphere of Accomplishment. I shall now further explain the characteristics for the accomplishment of mantras by those who practice yoga.
If one were to explain it in full detail,
it would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon;
only a Buddha is able to expound it.
If there is a practitioner of yoga who recites this one hundred thousand or ten million times, they will certainly attain accomplishment.
When desiring to achieve accomplishment:
First, one should [contemplate] the seven kinds of auspicious and sublime realms;
then, it is certain that the practitioner (*yogin*) will swiftly attain *siddhi*.

First, in a dream, one sees entering the Great Secret Maṇḍala of the Samaya-Assembly of the Mudrās of the Great Wish-Fulfilling, Vast, and Sovereign Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa of the Tathāgata Vairocana, who pervades all buddha-fields in the ten directions and all Buddhas of the three times.
We, all the Tathāgatas, shall bestow the chapter on the ground of the samādhi of the maṇḍala-seal empowerment.
We, the Tathāgatas, shall simultaneously praise [it] with one voice, saying:
Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
You have attained the gate of simultaneous opening to all buddha-fields of the ten directions;
you may roam at will through those various buddha-lands.
Each was empowered by the mindfulness of ninety-nine billion *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka-koṭi-nayuta-śata-sahasra* Tathāgatas,
thereby attaining such a state.
Exert yourself with diligent vigor;
do not engage in grasping or rejecting.

Second, he dreamed that he entered the assembly within the palace of the Samaya-mandala of the Great Maṇi-ratna Uṣṇīṣa, the Sovereign Buddha-Crown of the Great Lotus Lineage, amidst all the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time in all the buddha-fields of the ten directions.

I, all the Tathāgatas, bestow this chapter on the Samaya of the Mudrās and Maṇḍala for the Great Consecration of the Great Maṇi Jewel of the Uṣṇīṣa, the Venerable and Victorious One of the Great Lotus Family.
Upon attaining the Chapter on the Seal of the Great Maṇi Initiation Maṇḍala of the Sovereign Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa of All Tathāgatas,
all the Tathāgatas before me spoke with one voice, praising me, saying:
Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
You have obtained the *Samaya* chapter on the seal of the empowerment maṇḍala of the Exalted Buddha-uṣṇīṣa of the Great Lotus lineage.
Being sustained and empowered by all the Tathāgatas,
[he entered] the third dream: the samaya of the Great Maṇi Seal,

wherein he entered the samaya of the seals of the consecration maṇḍala of the Great Maṇi Jewel of the Uṣṇīṣa, the most Victorious Buddha-Crown of the Great Vajra Family of all the Tathāgatas of the three times in all the buddha-fields of the ten directions.
We, the Tathāgatas, have bestowed upon you this chapter on the Samaya of the Mudrās and Maṇḍala for the Consecration of the Great Maṇi Jewel of the Uṣṇīṣa, the Most Victorious of the Vajra Family;
and we have also bestowed upon us this chapter on the Samaya of the Dhāraṇī of the Uṣṇīṣa, the Most Victorious of the Vajra Family of all Tathāgatas.
All the Vajras raised their voices in unison and praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
You have attained the Samaya Chapter of the Great Maṇi-ratna Maṇḍala Seal of the Uṣṇīṣa, the Sovereign of the Vajra Family of all Tathāgatas."
He attained the samaya of the Great Maṇi-ratna Vajra-mudrā, which is the empowerment and protection bestowed by all the Vajras.

Fourth, he dreamed that he entered the Samaya Section of the Mudrās of the Great Consecration Maṇḍala of the Exalted Lineage of the Great Maṇi-ratnas of all Tathāgatas throughout the three times in all lands of the ten directions.

Behold this *samaya* of the secret accomplishment of the mudrās of the consecration maṇḍala of the Great Maṇi-jewel Banner, the Sovereign Buddha-uṣṇīṣa of the Noble Lineage of the Great Maṇi-jewel of all Tathāgatas.
All the Tathāgatas praised him with one voice, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
You have now obtained this 'Secret Heart Chapter on the Mudrās of the Empowerment Maṇḍala of the Supreme Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa of the Great Maṇi-Jewel Lineage of All Tathāgatas.'"
This empowerment rite is the Samaya Chapter of the Secret Heart Mantra of the Great Wish-Fulfilling Jewel Family of all Tathāgatas. It bestows manifest empowerment.

Fifth, he dreamed that he entered the secret maṇḍala of the samaya of the mudrās of the supreme great empowerment of the non-retrogressive wheel of all Tathāgatas throughout the three times in all the buddha-fields of the ten directions.
We Tathāgatas bestow upon you this chapter on the Samaya of the Secret Maṇḍala Mudrās for the Great Empowerment of Non-retrogression.
We Tathāgatas, with one voice, proclaim:
Excellent, excellent, son of good family!

You have now obtained this Chapter on the Samaya of the Mudrās of the Secret Maṇḍala for the Great Consecration of the Invincible and Victorious Uṣṇīṣa of all Tathāgatas throughout the three times in all buddha-fields of the ten directions.

The sixth dream was that we saw all the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time in all the buddha-fields of the ten directions dwelling at the bodhi trees, seated upon the vajra-thrones, manifesting perfect enlightenment and performing the rites of consecration for the stage of the Great Dharma King.

They saw all the buddha-fields of the ten directions and all the Tathāgatas of the three times seated upon lion thrones, conferring upon them the empowerment of the stage of the non-retrogressive Dharma King of all Tathāgatas.
Then all the Tathāgatas praised him with one voice, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!

O Resolute One, you have now received the empowerment of the Dharma King of non-retrogression from all Tathāgatas; we shall protect and mind you, so that you may firmly uphold this and never abandon it."
Seventh, he dreamed that the Tathāgata Śākyamuni was beneath the Bodhi tree,
seated upon the Vajrāsana,
emitting a great radiance.
He turns the Great Wheel of Dharma,
kindles the Great Torch of Dharma,
and rains down the Great Rain of Dharma.
They raise the great banner of the Dharma,
blow the great conch of the Dharma,
and beat the great drum of the Dharma.
It subdues the great armies of Māra.

Furthermore, it contains the chapter on the Samaya of the Mudrās of the Supreme Great Secret Maṇḍala for Bestowing Empowerment, which appears in all the Buddha-lands of the ten directions and beneath the Bodhi trees of all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time as they sit upon the Vajrāsana and turn the Great Wheel of Dharma while subduing the great armies of Māra.
He attained the chapter on the Secret Maṇḍala Seal and Samaya Seal of the Great Empowerment for Turning the Wheel of Dharma conferred by the Tathāgatas.
Then, all the Tathāgatas praised him with one voice, saying:
Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
You have attained the mantra-jewel, the firm liberation, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, the great empowerment, and the samaya of the secret maṇḍala mudrā.
In this manner, one should constantly and diligently apply oneself with sincerity to the Buddha-yoga meditation according to the Dharma,
upholding, receiving, reading,
and reciting it without ever ceasing or neglecting it.
Then one shall obtain these seven great auspicious dreams,
thereby realizing my *Sarvatathāgata-uṣṇīṣavijayā*, the Honored Sovereign of the Five Uṣṇīṣa Kings,
also known as the Mantra of the Miraculous Transformation of the Uṣṇīṣavijayā King that Dispels Obstacles.

One should enter the Samaya Assembly of the Great Mandala Seal of the Vairocana Tathāgata, the Sovereign Wheel-King of the Uṣṇīṣas of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Entering the gateway of the samaya of all places,

one beholds all the buddha-fields of the ten directions and all the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, including the Sovereign Victorious Uṣṇīṣa King Mahāvairocana Tathāgata and the four pāramitās.
And [there were] the Tathāgata Akṣobhya of the east, Vajradhara Guhyapati, and others;
the Tathāgata Ratnasambhava of the south, Gaganaratna, and others;
and the Tathāgata Amitāyus of the west, Padmanetra, and others.
In the north are the Tathāgata Amoghasiddhi, Viśvakarman, and others;
the four wisdoms and the four samayas,
along with the subtle and wondrous form-bodies of immeasurable holy assemblies.

One should reverently make offerings and uphold all the names of the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana, the Great Uṣṇīṣa, who is most honored and supreme throughout all the buddha-fields of the ten directions and all three periods of time.

One shall then attain the foremost among all the Samaya-dhāraṇī-siddhi-vidhi-paṭala of supernatural powers, including the seals and dhāraṇīs such as the *Vighnāntaka-uṣṇīṣa*, bestowed by the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana, the Most Honored and Victorious Uṣṇīṣa of all Buddhas throughout the three periods of time in all lands of the ten directions.
If there are all past transgressions—whether the ten non-virtues, the five heinous crimes, or the four grave offenses—that have been burning and persisting, they shall be extinguished and eliminated.

If there are sentient beings who, wherever they may be, hear this Great Consecration Light King, the Sovereign Uṣṇīṣa Cakra King mantra, one, two, three, or seven times passing through their faculty of hearing;
One will immediately attain the eradication of all karmic obstructions.
If there are practitioners who take pity on all sentient beings within the six realms of existence,
they should each prostrate toward the ten directions from the summit of a high mountain.
Each shall recite the Uṣṇīṣavijaya Dhāraṇī once.
All sentient beings within the range of one’s vision shall be entirely liberated from all sinful suffering and shall be reborn in the land of Akṣobhya Buddha.
Alternatively, one may write [the mantra] upon a banner and install it on the high peak of a mountain,
erecting a banner-pole with the banner suspended from its top;
in whichever direction the tail of the banner points, [that is the place].
The ten non-virtuous actions, the five heinous crimes, the four grave offenses,
